sites.name: Museum and Library of Alexandria
sites.summary: Ptolemaic research institute in the palace quarter, with salaried scholars and a library said to hold 400,000-700,000 rolls. Caesar's fire of 48 BC burned books (Seneca says 40,000, probably warehouse stock near the harbour). The Museum survived under Roman emperors, who appointed its members (Claudius added a wing); Aurelian's destruction of the Bruchion in 272 probably ended it. The daughter library in the Serapeum went with the temple in 391; the story of the Arab caliph burning it is a 13th-century fabrication.

sites.name: Library of Pergamon
sites.summary: Attalid library beside the sanctuary of Athena, rival of Alexandria; Pliny and Varro tell how a Ptolemaic ban on papyrus exports drove Pergamon to perfect parchment (pergamena). Plutarch reports, doubtfully, that Antony gave its 200,000 volumes to Cleopatra.

sites.name: Bibliotheca Ulpia
sites.summary: Twin libraries for Greek and Latin books flanking Trajan's Column in his Forum, dedicated 112-113, where the Historia Augusta claims to have consulted linen books and senatorial records. Sidonius Apollinaris was honoured with a statue here c. 456.

sites.name: Library of Asinius Pollio
sites.summary: Rome's first public library, founded by Gaius Asinius Pollio from the spoils of his Illyrian triumph in the Atrium Libertatis, realising Caesar's unfinished plan (entrusted to Varro). Augustus soon added the Palatine and Porticus Octaviae libraries.

sites.name: Library of Celsus, Ephesus
sites.summary: Built c. 114-117 by Tiberius Julius Aquila as library and tomb for his father, the consul and proconsul Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, buried in a sarcophagus beneath the reading room, with an endowment of 25,000 denarii for books. Burned c. 262; its façade was re-erected in 1970-78.

sites.name: Library of Hadrian, Athens
sites.summary: Colonnaded court of 100 columns with book rooms, built by Hadrian c. 132; Pausanias admired its alabaster and gilded roof. Damaged by the Herulians in 267 and later rebuilt as a church.

sites.name: Villa of the Papyri, Herculaneum
sites.summary: Seaside villa, probably of Caesar's father-in-law Piso Caesoninus, buried in 79 with some 1,800 carbonised rolls, chiefly the Epicurean works of Philodemus of Gadara. Since 2023 machine-learning on CT scans has begun to read unopened rolls.

sites.name: Library of Rogatianus, Thamugadi
sites.summary: Public library given by Marcus Julius Quintianus Flavius Rogatianus for 400,000 sesterces in the 3rd century, with a semicircular reading room and niches for book cupboards, among the few excavated provincial libraries.

sites.name: Library of Caesarea
sites.summary: Origen's library, enlarged by the martyr Pamphilus (d. 310) to some 30,000 volumes, where Origen produced the Hexapla and Eusebius wrote his histories. Jerome consulted it; it probably disappeared with the Arab conquest of Caesarea in 640-641.

sites.name: Qumran
sites.summary: Settlement on the Dead Sea associated with the scrolls found in nearby caves from 1947: about 900 manuscripts, including the oldest biblical texts and sectarian works often linked to the Essenes. Destroyed by the Romans in 68.
sites.debate: Whether the settlement housed the sect that owned the scrolls is debated.

sites.name: Nag Hammadi codices
sites.summary: Thirteen leather-bound papyrus codices buried in a jar near the Pachomian monasteries c. 350-400 and found in 1945, with 52 mostly Gnostic texts in Coptic, including the Gospel of Thomas. Their cartonnage includes documents from the 340s.

sites.name: Oxyrhynchus rubbish mounds
sites.summary: Rubbish mounds of a nome capital excavated by Grenfell and Hunt from 1896, yielding over 500,000 papyrus fragments: lost works of Sappho, Menander and Pindar, early Christian texts, and the paperwork of a Roman provincial town.

sites.name: Vindolanda tablets
sites.summary: Over 1,700 wooden leaf tablets from the fort's pre-Hadrianic phases, including strength reports, accounts, and Claudia Severa's birthday invitation to Sulpicia Lepidina, the earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman.
scholarship: Bowman & Thomas, The Vindolanda Writing Tablets I-III (1983-2003)

sites.name: Academy of Athens
sites.summary: Plato's school, sacked by Sulla in 86 BC; the old Academy ended then. A revived Neoplatonist school, based in private houses, flourished under Plutarch of Athens, Proclus (d. 485) and Damascius until Justinian's law of 529 banned pagans from teaching. Agathias says seven philosophers left for Persia c. 531 and returned disappointed under a treaty clause guaranteeing their safety.

sites.name: Law school of Berytus
sites.summary: The empire's leading law school, attested from the 3rd century, teaching in Latin until the 5th; Justinian recognised it in 533 as one of three official law schools. The earthquake and tsunami of 9 July 551 destroyed the city, and the school moved to Sidon.

sites.name: Auditoria of Kom el-Dikka, Alexandria
sites.summary: Some 20 horseshoe-shaped lecture halls excavated since 1980 near the baths, the physical setting of late antique Alexandrian teaching in philosophy, medicine and rhetoric, from Hypatia's successors to John Philoponus.
scholarship: Majcherek, in Derda et al., Alexandria: Auditoria of Kom el-Dikka (2007)

sites.name: Rhetorical schools of Rhodes
sites.summary: Rhodes taught Romans rhetoric and philosophy: Cicero studied with Apollonius Molon (78-77 BC) and Posidonius, Caesar sailed to study with Molon in 75 and was captured by pirates, and Tiberius lived here in voluntary exile 6 BC-AD 2, attending lectures.

sites.name: Massalia as university town
sites.summary: Strabo says Massalia had become a school for the Roman nobility, preferred to Athens, and Tacitus says Agricola studied there because it mixed Greek culture with provincial thrift.

sites.name: Maenian Schools of Augustodunum
sites.summary: Famous schools of Gaul, where Tacitus says sons of the Gallic nobility were held in 21. In 298 the rhetor Eumenius gave his salary of 600,000 sesterces to rebuild them, describing a portico with a painted world map.

sites.name: Schools of Burdigala
sites.summary: Ausonius' Commemoration of the Professors of Bordeaux portrays 26 teachers of grammar and rhetoric in the 4th century; Ausonius taught here for 30 years before becoming tutor to Gratian and consul in 379.

sites.name: Capitol school of Constantinople
sites.summary: Theodosius II's law of 27 February 425 established 31 salaried chairs (Greek and Latin grammar and rhetoric, philosophy, law) in the Capitol and banned private teachers from public halls.

sites.name: School of Libanius, Antioch
sites.summary: Libanius taught rhetoric at Antioch for 40 years from 354; his 64 orations and over 1,500 letters are the richest record of a late antique city. Pupils allegedly included John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia.

sites.name: School of the Persians, Edessa
sites.summary: School of Syriac theology founded by refugees from Nisibis after 363 (tradition credits Ephrem). It trained the clergy of the Persian church and translated Theodore of Mopsuestia; Zeno closed it in 489 as Nestorian.

sites.name: School of Nisibis
sites.summary: Refounded by Narsai after the Edessa school's expulsion, under Persian rule; its statutes of 496 and 590 survive. With up to 1,000 students it was the intellectual centre of the Church of the East.

sites.name: School of Gaza
sites.summary: Christian rhetorical school of Procopius of Gaza and his pupil Choricius, whose speeches describe the city's churches and defend the mime. A last flowering of classical oratory in Palestine.

sites.name: Schools of Carthage
sites.summary: The intellectual capital of Latin Africa, where Apuleius lectured and Augustine studied and taught rhetoric before leaving for Rome in 383, complaining of rowdy students (eversores).

sites.name: Schools of Tarsus
sites.summary: Strabo says Tarsus surpassed Athens and Alexandria in zeal for learning, though its students went abroad to finish; teachers included Athenodorus, tutor of Augustus, who reformed the city's government.

sites.name: Aphrodisias: sculptors and philosophers
sites.summary: Workshops of marble sculptors whose signatures appear in Rome and across the empire, and a school of philosophy: Alexander of Aphrodisias, the greatest commentator on Aristotle, held the imperial chair at Athens c. 200; late antique philosophers' busts survive.

sites.name: Yavneh (Jamnia)
sites.summary: Coastal town where, in rabbinic tradition, Yohanan ben Zakkai obtained Vespasian's permission to found an academy after 70; the sages of Yavneh reorganised Judaism without the Temple. The idea of a 'Council of Jamnia' fixing the biblical canon is a modern construction.

sites.name: Theatre of Aspendos
sites.summary: The best preserved Roman theatre, built by the architect Zeno under Marcus Aurelius for about 7,000, with its full scaenae frons standing; it served as a Seljuk caravanserai.

sites.name: Theatre of Arausio
sites.summary: Augustan theatre of the veteran colony with its stage wall 103 m long and 37 m high intact, and a niche for a statue of Augustus; Louis XIV called it 'the finest wall in my kingdom'.

sites.name: Theatre of Emerita
sites.summary: Built by Agrippa in 16-15 BC for the Lusitanian capital, seating about 6,000; its scaenae frons was rebuilt under Trajan or Hadrian and in the 4th century.

sites.name: Theatre of Sabratha
sites.summary: Severan theatre with a three-storey colonnaded stage front, rebuilt by Italian archaeologists in the 1930s; reliefs on the stage front show the Graces, the judgement of Paris and mime scenes. Damaged in the earthquake of 365.

sites.name: Great Theatre of Ephesus
sites.summary: Hellenistic theatre rebuilt under the empire for about 25,000; scene of the silversmiths' riot against Paul, when the crowd shouted 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians' for two hours.

sites.name: Theatre of Bostra
sites.summary: 2nd-century theatre of the capital of Arabia for about 9,000, preserved because Arabs and Ayyubids turned it into a fortress.

sites.name: Theatre of Thugga
sites.summary: Theatre given to his city in 168-169 by Publius Marcius Quadratus, a priest of the imperial cult, for 3,500 spectators, set into the hillside of an African town with Punic and Numidian roots.

sites.name: Hadrian's Villa (Tibur)
sites.summary: Hadrian's country palace below Tibur, built 118-138 over some 120 ha, with the Canopus, Maritime Theatre, Piazza d'Oro and buildings named, the Historia Augusta says, after the Lyceum, Academy, Prytaneum, Canopus, Poecile and Tempe. Later looted for sculpture.

sites.name: Villa del Casale, Piazza Armerina
sites.summary: Early 4th-century Sicilian villa with 3,500 m2 of mosaics: the Great Hunt corridor showing wild beasts captured in Africa and shipped for the games, the 'bikini girls' athletes, and the Labours of Hercules. The owner was a senatorial magnate, possibly a praefectus urbi; the attribution to Maximian is discredited.

sites.name: Fishbourne Palace
sites.summary: Palatial villa near Chichester built c. 75 with formal gardens, Italian marble and early mosaics, often attributed to the client king Tiberius Claudius Togidubnus. Burned c. 270.

sites.name: Chedworth villa
sites.summary: Large Cotswold villa with two bath suites, mosaics of the seasons and a water shrine whose stones were carved with chi-rhos, expanded in the 4th century, Britain's villa heyday.

sites.name: Villa Jovis, Capri
sites.summary: Tiberius' cliff-top palace on Capri, from which he ruled the empire from 27 until his death in 37; Suetonius tells of the 'Tiberius' leap' from which victims were thrown.

sites.name: Grotto of Tiberius at Sperlonga
sites.summary: Seaside villa whose dining grotto collapsed in AD 26 during Tiberius' dinner; Sejanus shielded him and won his trust. Its marble groups of Odysseus blinding Polyphemus and Scylla were found in 1957.

sites.name: Villa A, Oplontis
sites.summary: Luxury villa at Torre Annunziata with Second Style paintings, perhaps owned by Nero's wife Poppaea Sabina (an amphora addressed to her steward was found), buried in 79.

sites.name: Diocletian's Palace, Spalatum
sites.summary: Fortified retirement palace (c. 295-305) on the Dalmatian coast where Diocletian lived from 305 until his death c. 312, raising cabbages and refusing to return to power. Its walls hold the medieval town of Split; the mausoleum became the cathedral.

sites.name: Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad)
sites.summary: Fortified palace built by Galerius at his birthplace and named after his mother Romula; the tombs of Galerius and Romula are on the hill outside. An archivolt inscribed FELIX ROMVLIANA identified it in 1984.

sites.name: Villa of Livia at Prima Porta
sites.summary: Livia's villa 'ad Gallinas Albas', where an eagle dropped a white hen holding a laurel sprig into her lap, starting the laurel grove used for triumphal wreaths. Its painted garden room and the Prima Porta Augustus statue were found here.

sites.name: Villa of Chiragan
sites.summary: Huge villa on the Garonne that produced the largest collection of Roman portrait busts in France, including a series of emperors, now in the Musée Saint-Raymond in Toulouse.

sites.name: Centcelles
sites.summary: Villa near Tarraco whose domed hall has the earliest Christian dome mosaics, perhaps the mausoleum of the emperor Constans (d. 350).

sites.name: Villa of Carranque
sites.summary: Late 4th-century villa near Toletum with high-quality mosaics and a marble-clad hall, perhaps the property of Maternus Cynegius, praetorian prefect of Theodosius I.

sites.name: Ptolemy at Canopus
sites.summary: Ptolemy's dated observations in the Almagest run from 127 to 141; he set up an inscription at Canopus, near Alexandria, listing his astronomical constants (the Canobic Inscription, preserved in manuscripts).

sites.name: Hipparchus at Rhodes
sites.summary: Hipparchus made his observations at Rhodes from c. 147 to 127 BC, discovered the precession of the equinoxes, compiled a star catalogue of about 850 stars and founded trigonometry. Posidonius at Rhodes later measured the earth via Canopus' altitude.

sites.name: Horologium (Solarium) of Augustus
sites.summary: A meridian line on the Campus Martius, its gnomon the obelisk of Psammetichus II brought from Heliopolis in 10 BC. Pliny says the mathematician Novius Facundus designed it and that it had gone out of true in his day. Part of the bronze-lettered meridian was excavated in 1979-80.

sites.name: Tower of the Winds, Athens
sites.summary: Octagonal marble tower in the Roman Agora built by Andronicus of Cyrrhus, with sundials, a water clock and reliefs of the eight winds; Vitruvius describes its bronze Triton weathervane.

sites.name: Antikythera wreck
sites.summary: Wreck of a merchant ship of c. 70-60 BC off Antikythera, found by sponge divers in 1900, carrying bronzes and marbles for the Roman market and the Antikythera mechanism, a geared bronze calculator of solar, lunar and planetary cycles and eclipse dates.
